CycleAnalyzer · retrospective 2020-05-24 · model anchor 2020-04

DM+EM Cycle Monitor

Twenty-four economies read as mean-reverting cycles: where each one sits on the growth × inflation clock, what comes next and when, which cycles are not endangered, who stands apart from the global pack — and what all of it says to play in FX and yield curves.

Retrospective edition 2020-05-24. Information strictly before 00:00 Europe/Warsaw (2020-05-23T22:00:00Z). Monthly observations and their release vintages are separately dated below. Policy snapshots include only decisions already announced and effective. Negative FX funding costs are fully charged; a benign domestic cycle does not make a negative interest differential positive carry.

Reconstructed 2026-11-27 by applying the latest corrected methodology to historical inputs. The edition date identifies the information boundary; this is not a claim that these analyses or trades were published in 2020.

02Mean reversion & distance to danger

Each cycle variable is fit as an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. The projected path (OU decay plus fading momentum) is tested against two thresholds: the inflation-fight line (+1σ) and the recession zone (−1σ). An economy whose path never gets near either is flagged not in danger — the cycle has far to run before it is endangered.

03The context filter — which extremes to fade, which to leave alone

Mean reversion alone is a bad idea. A z-score says a variable is far from equilibrium; it says nothing about whether the forces that created the extreme are done. Every stretch is cross-examined against the prevailing context — leading growth momentum, policy direction, real-rate restrictiveness, the clock heading — and against its own turn evidence:

EARLY TURN — the correction has begun but has retraced only a fraction of the extreme, and the context says the cycle change is coming anyway. The best entry: the top is already in, you ride the rest.
SETUP — still pinned at the extreme, but the leading indicators are deteriorating hard from the top. The counter-movement has not printed yet — position before it does.
TREND INTACT — stretched, but the context still feeds the deviation (an early hiking cycle behind a rich currency). Do not fade: the statistical pull earns zero weight until the context breaks.
LATE — the reversion has mostly happened; the edge is gone.

06FX scorecard

Each currency is scored against the USD as the sum of five engines — carry + cycle + valuation + momentum − penalty. The engines are deliberately built on different sources of return, so the sum is less about magnitude than about agreement: any single engine can be wrong for a year, but a currency where four pull the same way is wrong far less often. Components are scaled to comparable size (each contributes roughly ±0.5 to ±1.5): a total above ≈ +1 is a serious long candidate, anything below ≈ −0.5 is funding-leg material.

The five engines, one by one

Carry

0.25 × policy-rate differential vs USD, clipped ±6pp; positive pickup halved only when inflation gap eats it; negative funding costs fully charged

What it measures
The annualized interest differential you are paid — or pay — just for holding the currency versus USD, before anything moves. It is the only component that accrues to you every day the view is *wrong but not very wrong*.

Where the edge lies
Uncovered interest parity says forwards should price away the differential, so carry should net to zero. Empirically it does not — the forward premium puzzle: high-carry currencies depreciate less, on average, than their forwards imply, so rolling forwards harvests a persistent risk premium. That premium is compensation for crash risk: you collect it in calm regimes and give a slice back in risk-off. The model's refinement is that *nominal* carry which merely compensates for higher inflation is not edge at all — it is the currency's expected depreciation in disguise — hence the haircut when the inflation gap swallows the pickup, and the separate penalty beyond that.

Where it fails
in global vol spikes: carry is a crowded trade and unwinds violently, all pairs at once, regardless of local merit.

Cycle

phase value (Overheating +0.9, Goldilocks +0.6, Stagflation −0.6, Disinflation −0.9) × cycle amplitude (capped 1.5) × 0.5; when the clock's ETA to the next phase ≤ 9 months, half the weight shifts to the *destination* phase

What it measures
Where the economy sits on the clock, and — more importantly — where it is rotating to. Overheating and Goldilocks attract capital: rate expectations climb, equity and credit inflows follow. Stagflation and Disinflation repel it: cuts are coming, growth is going.

Where the edge lies
Markets are good at pricing the central bank's *last* move and bad at pricing the *rotation*. A currency entering Overheating will receive hikes that are not yet in the forwards; one rolling into Disinflation will receive cuts that are not either. The heading blend is deliberate: when rotation is fast you want to own the currency for what the cycle is about to do, not for where it stands. Amplitude scaling keeps direction honest — an economy hovering near the origin of the clock has a direction but no cycle, and direction without amplitude is noise.

Where it fails
when a supply shock masquerades as a cycle phase: oil-shock stagflation is bullish for an oil exporter's currency and bearish for an importer's, and the clock cannot tell them apart.

Valuation

−0.45 × REER deviation from its 10y average (z, clipped ±2.5), multiplied by the context-filter gate: ×1.25 on EARLY TURN, ×1.0 on SETUP, ×0.5 on WATCH, ×0.3 on LATE, ×0 on TREND INTACT

What it measures
How rich or cheap the currency is in *real, trade-weighted* terms — the BIS broad REER against its own decade. Real, so inflation differentials are already netted out; effective, so it measures competitiveness against all partners, not just the dollar.

Where the edge lies
Real exchange rates mean-revert over multi-year horizons through the competitiveness channel: a persistently rich currency erodes exports and the current account until the currency itself gives way, and vice versa. But the half-lives are long, which is exactly why this component is the one the context filter polices hardest: a cheap currency whose central bank is cutting into a slowdown is cheap *for a reason* and earns nothing (TREND INTACT ×0); the same cheapness with the correction already underway and the cycle turning earns a premium (EARLY TURN ×1.25). Valuation is edge only near turning points — the gate is what turns a slow anchor into a timing-aware signal.

Where it fails
when the fair value itself moves: a terms-of-trade regime shift (commodity supercycle, an energy transition) makes the 10-year mean stale, and the model will call 'rich' what is actually a new equilibrium.

Momentum

policy direction: hiking +0.4, on hold 0, cutting −0.4; +0.2 bonus for hiking while inflation momentum is already falling

What it measures
Which way the central bank is actually moving right now — not the level of rates (that is carry) but the direction of travel.

Where the edge lies
Policy cycles persist: hikes cluster, cuts cluster, and the first move is rarely the last, while FX over one-to-six-month horizons follows the *change* in rate differentials more than the level. The bonus case is deliberate and is the strongest single configuration in the stack: a bank hiking while inflation already falls is delivering rising *real* rates — the currency gets the differential and the credibility at once.

Where it fails
at the end of the cycle: the last hike is historically a sell signal, not a buy — the clock and the danger model are the overlays meant to catch the turn this component misses.

Penalty

−0.6 per pp of inflation gap beyond +2pp above target, capped at −3

What it measures
A credibility discount, not a return forecast. Beyond a couple of points above target, inflation stops being an input to carry and becomes the whole story: pass-through accelerates, expectations de-anchor, and the real value of the carry collapses faster than the nominal rate can compensate.

Where the edge lies
The edge here is *avoidance*: the cap at −3 encodes that past a point the right reading is 'uninvestable', not 'great short'. Shorting a 30–40% yielder pays ruinous negative carry, so a broken-credibility currency is excluded from the crosses on *both* sides — you neither hold it for the carry trap nor short it for the bleed. It re-enters the tradable universe only when disinflation is delivered, at which point the (still huge) carry starts counting again.

Where it fails
at the moment of a credible stabilization: the penalty lags the regime change, and the first year of a successful disinflation is historically the best carry trade there is.

How to read the sum

  • The edge is in the agreement structure, not the total. Carry confirmed by cycle and momentum — being paid to hold a currency whose central bank is hiking into an overheating economy — is the strongest configuration in the framework. Carry against cycle (a high yielder rolling into Disinflation, where the coming cuts will eat the differential) is the classic carry trap, and the sum catches it automatically: the cycle term goes negative before the carry term does.
  • A single-engine score is a watchlist item, not a trade. A total driven by valuation alone is precisely the 'mean reversion alone' mistake the context filter exists to block; a total driven by carry alone deserves a credibility check before anything else.
  • Why crosses instead of USD legs. The scores are measured vs USD, but the cleanest expression pairs the strongest long against the weakest credible funder: the dollar — with its own cycle, its own politics — nets out, leaving a relative-cycle position. Its actual policy-rate differential can be positive or negative; forward basis and trading costs also matter.
  • The penalty is a filter, not a signal. A deeply negative penalty (TRY-style) removes the currency from both sides of the book: the carry is uncollectible and the short bleeds. Uninvestable is a verdict too.
Worked example — MXN, this month's top score (+0.93): carry +1.34 from a +5.4pp policy-rate pickup over USD; cycle -0.01 from sitting in Goldilocks and heading to Disinflation in ~2m; valuation +0.00 from a REER -0.8σ vs its decade, credited because the context verdict is TREND_INTACT; momentum -0.40 because Banxico is cutting. 1 engines pull for it, momentum against. The agreement structure, not any single number, is the trade.

The scorecard

Model crosses — strongest longs against the weakest credible funders (a broken-credibility high-carry currency is excluded from the short leg: shorting 30–40% carry is a bleed, not a hedge):

  • Long MXN / short JPY — edge +1.95. buy MXN, sell JPY via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +5.6pp annualized, before forward basis and costs
  • Long BRL / short PLN — edge +1.60. buy BRL, sell PLN via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +2.5pp annualized, before forward basis and costs
  • Long ZAR / short CZK — edge +1.54. buy ZAR, sell CZK via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +3.5pp annualized, before forward basis and costs

07What is most interesting to play

Each play states the exact legs to put on and the context check that licenses it — a stretch alone never does.

PLAY 1

Euro area curve steepener

The Euro area 10y−policy slope sits at +0.55pp (-1.1σ vs its own history, half-life 22m). The economy is in Disinflation, which pushes the slope steeper. Crucially, the move has *already started* but only 33% of the extreme is retraced — you are not calling the turn, the turn is in, and the context says the rest is coming. Why not South Africa, whose slope is more stretched (+1.9σ)? Because its stretch is TREND INTACT — SARB is still cutting, which keeps feeding the steepness — and a confirmed trend is precisely the extreme this framework refuses to fade on statistics alone.

How to express it
2s10s steepener in EUR: receive 2y swap (or long 2y govvies), pay 10y — DV01-neutral, so the P&L is the slope, not the level.

Context check
stretch -1.1σ, already turning, 33% retraced; context score +0.60 → EARLY_TURN: the correction has started but only 33% of the extreme is unwound, and the surrounding cycle context points the same way — the rest of the move is the trade.

Risk — A new growth or inflation shock can alter the phase, policy path and term premium. The measured slope is 10y minus policy, not an observed 2s10s spread; the 2s10s expression requires separate execution pricing and DV01 sizing.

PLAY 2

Long MXN / short JPY

The widest credible model-score gap is +1.95. Long MXN: carry +1.34, cycle -0.01 (Goldilocks), valuation +0.00, momentum -0.40, credibility component +0.00. Banxico's calendar-based policy stance is cutting. Short JPY: carry -0.06, cycle -0.68 (Disinflation), valuation -0.28, momentum +0.00, credibility component +0.00. BoJ's calendar-based policy stance is on hold. The indicative annual policy-rate differential is +5.60pp before forward basis and costs. A negative differential is a funding cost that the cycle/valuation view must overcome. The cross expresses a relative-currency view; the score is a heuristic, not a forecast return.

How to express it
buy MXN, sell JPY via 3m FX forwards (rolled); indicative positive policy-rate differential +5.6pp annualized, before forward basis and costs.

Context check
long leg REER: stretch -0.8σ, still pinned at the extreme; context score -0.58 → TREND_INTACT: the extreme is CONFIRMED by the prevailing context — the forces that created it are still in place; do not fade this on statistics alone. Short leg REER: no meaningful stretch — this leg is not a mean-reversion bet.

Risk — a global risk-off compresses EM carry crosses regardless of local cycles; the short leg rallies on safe-haven flows.

PLAY 3

The fresh signal: Poland

NBP keeps cutting while inflation is above target and re-accelerating (+2.3pp over 3m) — credibility risk, watch the currency. This is the 'one fresh signal' class of trade: the model singles out a policy divergence. A trade requires that this divergence is not already reflected in market prices; the monthly inputs do not measure forwards or the distribution of gains and losses.

How to express it
sell PLN vs a credible regional peer via forwards and put on a 2s10s steepener — easing into rising inflation ends with a weaker currency and a front-end repricing.

Context check
this is a divergence/momentum trade, not a fade: already inside the inflation-fight zone, with inflation momentum +2.3pp over 3m — the context is moving *with* the position, which is what the filter requires when there is no extreme to revert.

Risk — single-meeting risk — one CPI print or one MPC vote can void the divergence; keep it tactical.

PLAY 4

The reckoning trade: Poland front-end inflation repricing risk

A central bank holding a negative real rate (-4.2%) with inflation +2.2pp above target and momentum +2.3pp/3m eventually validates the market's fear, not its hope. The trade is in the front end, not the currency: PLN is a second-order long *if* the bank moves, a short if it keeps refusing — so let rates carry the view.

How to express it
pay 2y PLN swap (or short 2y govvies / front-end futures); keep duration elsewhere until the front end reprices the hikes.

Context check
this is a divergence/momentum trade, not a fade: already inside the inflation-fight zone, with inflation momentum +2.3pp over 3m — the context is moving *with* the position, which is what the filter requires when there is no extreme to revert.

Risk — the bank may be right — if growth cracks first, inflation dies on its own and paying the front end loses.

08Methodology

Clock
Growth z = OECD composite leading indicator's deviation from 100, scaled by 15y dispersion. Inflation z = CPI y/y minus the central-bank target, scaled likewise. Phase angle θ = atan2(infl, growth); rotation = median monthly Δθ over 9m.
Mean reversion
AR(1)/OU fit per series; expected path blends OU decay with fading 3-month momentum (the realistic rise-then-revert hump). Danger = the projected path crossing +1σ (inflation) or −1σ (growth); safe requires staying 0.6σ clear for 36 months.
Context filter
Every |z| ≥ 0.75 stretch is cross-examined: turn evidence (3m drift back toward the mean, share of the 12m peak already retraced) plus a context score from leading-growth momentum, real-rate restrictiveness, policy direction and the clock heading. Verdicts gate the mean-reversion terms in the trade models: TREND INTACT zeroes them, EARLY TURN boosts them.
Standouts
6m policy change vs universe median (robust MAD z), real-rate gap vs own decade, 3m inflation momentum → early hiker, deliberating hike, cutting into inflation, behind the curve, room to cut.
Data
Explicit historical input matrices only. The reviewed source ledger and country observation dates below govern this edition; the present-day repository cache is not an input.

Historical inputs and timing

Information cutoff: before 24 May 2020, 00:00 Europe/Warsaw (2020-05-23T22:00:00Z). Reconstructed on 2026-11-27. No archive of the present-day sources reaches back to 2020, so every input is either a real-time vintage, a decision history dated to the day, or a present-day history cut at an explicit, conservative publication gate; each one, with its availability bound, is in the ledger below. Projected paths are model scenarios, not realised outcomes.

Growth. 21 growth inputs are OECD composite leading indicators, amplitude adjusted, exactly as published in the April 2020 edition of the OECD real-time revisions database (Main Economic Indicators vintages, never revised afterwards; latest reference month 2020-03). That edition is used because its CLI was public by 2020-04-30 (edition month end (conservative rule)). Evidence: edition month end. Chile, Colombia and Thailand have no real-time leading indicator and no growth input; an input whose latest observation is more than 9 months older than the anchor month is not used (data notes below).

Inflation. Headline CPI y/y for 21 economies is computed inside a single real-time vintage: the OECD consumer-price index of the April 2020 edition, the newest edition whose month had ended before the cutoff (a conservative bound; no earlier publication date is claimed). China’s series is stored in this edition as a fixed-base index, so its y/y is the 12-month ratio inside the vintage; because that derived index can deviate from the published y/y, the published y/y behind the one-full-month gate competes and the fresher series is used (here the published y/y). Australia and New Zealand publish quarterly CPI, repeated across each quarter’s three months. The United States uses the BLS CPI-U all-items NSA index from the ALFRED 2020-05-22 (Friday) vintage, latest 2020-04. Chile, Colombia and Thailand, and China (published y/y fresher than the vintage index), and India (its vintage series is the CPI for Industrial Workers, not the Combined CPI the RBI targets) use the present-day BIS CPI history requested only through 2020-03: a reference month is admitted once the whole following month has passed, although these offices publish within about ten days. Headline CPI y/y is rarely revised, but those histories are not vintages. Newer national releases that were public before the cutoff but are absent from the eligible vintage are not inserted, so an older observation date does not mean no newer release existed.

Exchange rates and yields. No vintage of the BIS broad real effective exchange rates for 2020 is retrievable. All 24 REER histories are present-day BIS broad indices requested only through 2020-03 (one full month after each reference month, against BIS publication around mid-month). Their later revisions — updated trade weights, revised consumer prices, a wider basket — are not removed; REER enters the model only through the valuation leg of the FX score. The 17 ten-year government yields are monthly market averages through 2020-04, the last completed month; market yields were observable as the month ended and are not revised.

Policy. Monthly policy histories are BIS end-of-month policy rates through 2020-04, the last completed month. The current effective snapshot is the rate in force on 2020-05-23 in the BIS daily decision history (downloaded only to that day): decisions announced but not yet effective at the cutoff are excluded. Policy rates are administrative facts, public when set, and are not revised. Changes are measured from the snapshot to exact completed-month anchors (3m: 2020-01, 6m: 2019-10, 12m: 2019-04). Policy instruments are those of the time (see the table); Mexico’s BIS series is the overnight interbank rate, a daily market rate until Banxico targeted it. Indicative carry is a policy-rate differential, not an executable forward quote; the curve input is the 10y yield minus the matched-month policy rate, not a traded 2s10s spread. OU horizons start at each series’ last eligible observation, so ETAs are not countdowns from the edition date.

Source observations missing inside the histories (no values are filled): policy/JP: 1999-03, 1999-04, 1999-05, 1999-06, 1999-07, 1999-08 … 70 more through 2006-02; y10/MX: 2001-08, 2001-09, 2001-11, 2007-10, 2008-02, 2008-05 … 45 more through 2020-03.

Inflation benchmarks are those publicly in force at the cutoff and are held constant through each historical fit. Where an official objective refers to an index other than headline CPI (the Federal Reserve's PCE price index; see each row), the benchmark is applied to headline CPI. India's benchmark is the RBI's stated CPI objective for the current period. Benchmarks apply to the headline CPI series used here. Each benchmark is the target for the current calendar year as publicly known at the cutoff; China's is the government's annual CPI objective, announced each March (until then the previous year's applies). Where a range was set, its midpoint is used; for the euro area's ‘below but close to 2%’, 1.9%. Sources are listed only if published on or before the edition’s last eligible day.

The CBRT's Monetary and Exchange Rate Policy for 2018 (5 Dec 2017, para 2) had set the 5 percent target for the three-year period beginning in 2018 'as per the agreement reached with the government'. Growth input definitions

United States: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA USA); Euro area: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, euro-area aggregate as published, database code EA19); Japan: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA JPN); United Kingdom: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA GBR); Canada: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA CAN); Australia: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA AUS); Switzerland: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the February 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA CHE; not carried by the April 2020 edition); Sweden: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA SWE); Norway: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the February 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA NOR; not carried by the April 2020 edition); New Zealand: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the February 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA NZL; not carried by the April 2020 edition); China: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA CHN); India: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA IND); Brazil: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA BRA); Mexico: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the February 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA MEX; not carried by the April 2020 edition); South Africa: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA ZAF); Turkiye: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA TUR); Poland: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA POL); Hungary: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA HUN); Czechia: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA CZE); Indonesia: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA IDN); Korea: OECD composite leading indicator, amplitude adjusted, as published in the April 2020 edition (real-time database, LI_AA KOR); Chile, Colombia, Thailand: no real-time growth input.

Data notes: cli/XM, cpi/XM: from the February 2015 edition the real-time database carries the euro-area aggregate as EA19 (Lithuania joined the euro area on 1 January 2015) instead of EA18; the aggregate is used as published. cli/CH: the April 2020 edition carries no CHE leading indicator; the newest earlier eligible edition carrying it (February 2020, through 2019-12) is used. cli/NO: the April 2020 edition carries no NOR leading indicator; the newest earlier eligible edition carrying it (February 2020, through 2019-12) is used. cli/NZ: the April 2020 edition carries no NZL leading indicator; the newest earlier eligible edition carrying it (February 2020, through 2019-11) is used. cli/MX: the April 2020 edition carries no MEX leading indicator; the newest earlier eligible edition carrying it (February 2020, through 2019-12) is used. cpi/CN: the April 2020 CPI edition stores a fixed-base index (y/y = 12-month ratio inside the vintage); the published y/y behind the one-full-month publication gate competes, and the published y/y (latest 2020-03) is used as the fresher series. cpi/IN: the real-time database's India series is the CPI for Industrial Workers, while the RBI's 4% objective refers to the all-India Combined CPI; the present-day BIS Combined CPI history behind the one-full-month publication gate (latest 2020-03) is used, not the April 2020 vintage index. policy/JP: the BIS daily series is blank from 2013-04-04 to 2016-09-20; months without a BIS row carry the last BIS level as a proxy. From 2016-02-16 the rate applied to Policy-Rate Balances, -0.10% (announced 2016-01-29; source below the policy decisions), fills the blank days; the BIS series resumes at the same level on 2016-09-21. policy/CN: the one-year loan prime rate (LPR) became the policy rate on 2019-08-20 (the BIS series switches from the one-year benchmark lending rate, 4.35% → 4.25%). The switch is an instrument change, not a decision on the benchmark rate, which was retained at 4.35%; the first fixing of the new reference rate was 0.10pp lower, and that gap is not counted as a policy move (PBoC Announcement [2019] No. 15 (signed 16 Aug, posted 17 Aug 2019): from 20 Aug 2019 the National Interbank Funding Center publishes the loan prime rate on the 20th of each month, and banks are to price new loans mainly off it ('各银行应在新发放的贷款中主要参考贷款市场报价利率定价'); the PBoC's Q&A of the same day: 'the benchmark deposit and lending rates are retained'; first new one-year LPR, 20 Aug 2019: 4.25%): earlier history is spliced by -0.10pp so that policy changes are measured on the new instrument. policy/IN: BIS monthly differs from the daily month-end in 2007-03; monthly rows retained. policy/TR: the one-week repo rate became the policy rate on 2010-05-20 (the BIS series switches from the overnight borrowing rate, 6.50% → 7.00%). The switch is not a rate change (CBRT Monetary Policy Committee decision No. 2010-16, 18 May 2010: overnight rates kept unchanged; as a 'technical rate adjustment', 'the one week repo rate, which becomes the new policy rate, is set at 7 percent—50 basis points above the overnight borrowing rates'): earlier history is spliced by +0.50pp so that policy changes are measured on the new instrument. policy/ID: the BI 7-Day (Reverse) Repo Rate became the policy rate on 2016-08-19 (the BIS series switches from the BI Rate, 6.50% → 5.25%). The switch is not a rate change (Bank Indonesia press release No. 18/67/DKom, 19 Aug 2016: the Board of Governors (18–19 Aug 2016) held the BI 7-day Reverse Repo Rate at 5.25% and, as announced on 15 Apr 2016, 'terhitung mulai hari ini Bank Indonesia menggunakan BI 7-day RR Rate sebagai suku bunga kebijakan menggantikan BI Rate' (from today the BI 7-day RR Rate replaces the BI Rate as the policy rate); the BI Rate had stood at 6.50%): earlier history is spliced by -1.25pp so that policy changes are measured on the new instrument. policy/TH: the BIS daily series shows 0.50% on 2020-05-06 only, between 0.75% on 2020-05-05 and 2020-05-07; no decision was announced, so that day is read at 0.75% (a one-day data error, not a policy move).
